chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Buying property as a couple is a great step - and an important legal decision. Especially for common-law couples, whose rights differ from those of married couples, it is essential to properly structure the purchase to protect yourself.

This guide covers ways to hold property jointly, the importance of an agreement, and the protections to provide.

Informative content, not legal advice: consult a notary. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

Buying as a couple is a great step - and an important legal decision, especially for common-law couples, whose rights differ from those of married couples. This guide covers ways of holding together, the importance of an agreement and the protections to provide.

Informative content, not legal advice: consult a notary.

chapters.title: Married and common-law partners
chapters.html:
Understand why status changes everything.

In Quebec, married or civilly united couples benefit from protection rules (family heritage) which surround the family residence.

The de facto spouses, they do not have not these automatic protections: in the event of separation or death, their rights depend above all on what is writes (title, agreement, will).

Many common-law partners are unaware of this reality - and discover it at the worst time.

In Quebec, married and civil unions benefit from protections for family assets; de facto spouses, no - their rights depend mainly on the writing (title, agreement, will). Many people ignore it and discover it at the worst time: for an unmarried couple, everything depends on the documents.

Emilie's advice

“We've been together for 15 years, it's like a marriage. » No: in Quebec, de facto union does not create the same rights. For an unmarried couple, everything depends on the documents.

chapters.title: How to hold property
chapters.html:
Choose the holding structure.

How to register the property on title is a decision structuring :

  • In joint ownership, in equal shares (50/50) or according to each person's contribution.
  • The title must clearly reflect who owns what.

If only one spouse has title, the other may find themselves without rights to the property - even after years and numerous payments. Make this choice with full knowledge of the facts.

The way of registering the property in the title is structuring: in joint ownership, in equal shares or according to the contribution of each person. If only one spouse is on title, the other may find themselves without rights - even after years of payments. If you pay half, make sure you get the title.

Emilie's advice

If you pay half the mortgage, make sure you're on title. Contributing financially without appearing on the title is the classic scenario where you lose everything when you separate.

chapters.title: The agreement between spouses
chapters.objective: Plan for the unexpected in writing.
chapters.html:
Plan for the unexpected in writing.

An agreement (often a joint ownership agreement or a cohabitation contract) specifies in advance what could otherwise be settled in court:

  • The distribution of shares.
  • Who pays what (mortgage, taxes, maintenance).
  • What happens in the event of separation (purchase, sale, deadlines).
  • What happens in the event of death (with the will).

It's a bit like insurance: you hope you'll never use it, but it avoids painful conflicts.

An agreement (of joint ownership or cohabitation) specifies in advance what would otherwise be settled in court: distribution of shares, who pays what, and what happens in the event of separation or death. Write it when everything is going well, not in the middle of a breakup.

Emilie's advice

Write the agreement WHEN things are going well, not when things are going badly. Calmly discussing the “what if one day…” when purchasing is infinitely simpler than in the middle of a breakup.

chapters.title: Protecting the survivor: will and insurance
chapters.objective: Also think about the death, not just the breakup.
chapters.html:
Also think about the death, not just the breakup.

For de facto spouses especially, the death of one partner can leave the other in a precarious situation if there is nothing planned.

  • Will : without it, a de facto spouse does not automatically inherit.
  • Life insurance : can allow the survivor to repurchase the share or repay the mortgage.
  • Clause in the agreement : coordinate with the will.

These tools, put in place together, form a real safety net.

Also think about death: without a will, a common-law partner does not automatically inherit. Life insurance can allow the survivor to buy back the share or repay the mortgage, avoiding a fire sale. Coordinate agreement, will and insurance.

Emilie's advice

Life insurance that covers the balance of the mortgage prevents the survivor from having to sell in disaster. This is often one of a couple's best peace of mind purchases.

chapters.title: Buying together, step by step
chapters.html:
Structure the purchase calmly.

For a well-planned purchase for two, follow this logical order:

  1. Clarify your status and your real protections.
  2. Decide on distribution of shares.
  3. Have a written convention by a notary.
  4. Update your wills accordingly.
  5. Register the property in title in accordance with the agreement.

A little rigor at the start protects your relationship - and your assets - for a long time.

For a well-planned joint purchase: clarify your status, decide on the distribution, have an agreement drawn up by a notary, update your wills, and register the property on the title in accordance with the agreement. It's not a lack of trust, it's mutual respect.

Emilie's advice

Treat the purchase together as a small joint project: a written agreement, clear roles, up-to-date documents. It's not a lack of trust, it's mutual respect.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Clarify our status and our real protections.
  2. Decide on the distribution of shares.

Within 30 days

  1. Have an agreement drawn up by a notary.
  2. Update our wills accordingly.

Then

  1. Register the property on title in accordance with our agreement.

To structure well

  1. Clarify our status and decide on the distribution of shares.
  2. Have an agreement drawn up and our wills updated.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Family assets: protections for married couples/civil unions.
  • De facto spouses: without automatic protections; the written word takes precedence.
  • Joint ownership: joint ownership, in equal shares or according to contribution.
  • Joint ownership agreement: agreement regulating shares, payments and exits.
  • Property title: must reflect the real agreement of the couple.
  • Family assets: protections for married couples/civil unions.
  • De facto spouses: without automatic protections; the written word takes precedence.
  • Joint ownership: joint ownership, in equal shares or according to contribution.
  • Joint ownership agreement: agreement regulating shares, payments and exits.
  • Property title: must reflect the real agreement of the couple.
